sources.text:
US northwest battles wildfires after Spokane neighborhoods scorched
Wildfires supercharged by drought and intense heat tore through the northwestern US city of Spokane, forcing the evacuation of 65,000 people and reducing hundreds of buildings to cinders, as firefighters raced Monday to contain the flames.
Aerial flybys revealed somewhere between 700-1,110 structures have been lost since the fires broke out over the weekend, authorities said, with anxious families awaiting news about when they could return.
Three fires have combined to burn 8,026 acres in the Spokane area of Washington state according to InciWeb, a federal interagency information system, with firefighters making use of cooler temperatures, higher humidities and thick smoke to make "significant gains" against two of them.
Local officials said so far no one has been reported hurt.
Cooler temperatures were expected Monday and Tuesday, though the respite will be brief, with a warming trend resuming mid-week that will raise temperatures into the mid to high-90's Fahrenheit with relative humidity in the lower teens.
Video of the fire aftermath on Sunday showed scores of homes burned to the ground, with only their brick fireplaces and foundations remaining, while other houses nearby escaped practically unscathed.
"Just driving around looking at the homes it's just one of the most heartbreaking things I've ever seen in my life," Spokane resident Geoff Beadles told AFP, after evacuating with his fiancee and two dogs.
- More frequent fires -
Authorities are attempting to make contact with 14 people whom they have failed to reach by cell phone but are not yet presumed missing, Sheriff John Nowels told a press conference Monday.
"I think the estimate is potentially up to 65,000 people we had to move out of these areas, and if you think about what that entails, the fact that we were able to get people out of those areas within several hours in an active fire zone is pretty incredible," said Nowels.
Mayor Lisa Brown said authorities were combing the city block by block to assess damages and potential reignition, and couldn't tell people yet when they could return home.
"It could be weeks, depending on where your home and property is," she said.
"I think from a historical standpoint, this is likely the worst natural disaster in Spokane's history," Washington Governor Bob Ferguson added.
Ferguson, who has been speaking with President Donald Trump, said he was awaiting the approval from the federal government of assistance including for search and rescue, debris removal, medical supplies and assistance, temporary sheltering and emergency power.
"I'm very optimistic that they will grant it, and hopefully very soon," he added.
Ferguson declared a state of emergency on August 1, citing drought conditions that have stretched four consecutive years, unusually high temperatures and high winds exacerbating record-setting wildfires.
Human-caused climate change is increasingly creating conditions for more frequent and intense wildfires, through increased heat, extended drought, and a "thirsty" atmosphere that enhances the drying of organic matter.
It is a vicious loop, with increased wildfires releasing massive amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, accelerating planetary warming.
- 'Extraordinary wildfire season' -
Fire officials warned that "unauthorized" drone incursions into restricted airspace above wildfires were forcing the grounding of helicopters and other aircraft fighting the blazes.
The head of Washington's Department of Natural Resources, David Upthegrove, said the fires in Spokane were among 16 major blazes burning throughout the state of Washington, covering 262,000 acres.
"This is an extraordinary fire season," he said.
An outage map published by local utility Avista showed over 6,445 customers were without power due to the fires as of early Monday.
The biggest of the three fires burning in Spokane, the Old Trails fire, jumped the Spokane River on Saturday afternoon and crossed into the city proper.
Another resident, Tena Risley, said she saw flames behind trees near her home and, in a panic, she grabbed her dog and a few things. She got stuck in traffic trying to flee as the fast-moving fires blocked routes out of the city.
"There were probably hundreds and hundreds of cars," she told AFP.

sources.news_title: Major wildfires spread in northwest US
sources.text:
Wildfires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area while destroying at least 600 homes, businesses and other structures, authorities said yesterday.
The fires in and around Spokane, the state’s second largest city, burned about 8.2 square miles (about 21km2) over the weekend and were among dozens of wildfires across the western US that severely taxed the ability of federal, state and local agencies to fight them.
About 390 square miles (1,010km2) has burned across the state, and some of the fires, including those in the Spokane area, are uncontained.
Photo: AP
No one is hurt or unaccounted for so far
Fire and law enforcement officials said there had been no reports of injuries or people unaccounted for — but they stressed it was early in the response effort.
Officials said that the evacuees in Spokane included patients at its US Veterans Affairs hospital.
Video from the Spokane area showed buildings on fire, black smoke billowing up near neighborhoods, and the smoking ruins of homes, with only chimneys still standing. Several officials expressed concern that the area does not appear likely to get a break in coming days from the weather, which is expected to remain dry.
“We are not out of danger,” US Senator Maria Cantwell said during a news conference in Spokane. “The next couple of days will be challenging.”
Investigators have not determined how the blazes started.
HIGH WINDS
High winds make it hard to fight fires in Spokane area
While temperatures Sunday in Spokane were forecast to remain below 80°F (27°C), wind gusts from 35mph to 45mph (56kph to 72kph) were expected, said Benjamin Cossel, public information officer for the federal response team from California called in to fight with the fires.
“We have weather working against us, and we have terrain working against us,” Cossel said.
There were three fires in the Spokane area: the Old Trails Fire, the Fairview Fire and the Meadowview Fire. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency Saturday and the US National Weather Service (NWS) issued a “particularly dangerous situation” red flag alert for eastern Washington.
Cossel said that as it gets warmer during the day, cool air that is closer to the ground and keeping winds at bay would rise, allowing winds to move through the area. The Spokane River cuts through the city of about 229,000 people and there are steep canyons on both sides that channel the wind.
“They push the fire through the canyons, up, up the slopes, and then outside the slopes and around,” he said. “It’s very very hilly, very very steep slopes, a lot of canyons that create really turbulent, really challenging sort of wind scenarios.”
Spokane sets up shelter for impacted residents
Authorities in Spokane set up a shelter at the city’s main convention center. About 400 people were staying there, officials said Sunday.
Spokane County Commissioner Chris Jordan said relatives of his were in an area affected by the fires and that they do not know if their home is still standing. He said he spoke with them as they were leaving the home.
“They’re in their car and all they can see is smoke everywhere, and it was incredibly scary for so many people,” he said during the news conference.
About 10,000 people had lost power, said the local power company.
Several larger fires continued to burn in less populated areas northwest of Spokane, including one about 80 miles (129km) from the city that has burned about 210 square miles (544km2). Another fire in eastern Oregon, about 70 miles (113km) to the northwest in the Stinkingwater Mountains, has burned about 336 square miles (870km2).
“The whole northwest is heavily impacted right now,” said Keila Vizcarra, the spokesperson for the federal team from California handling what has been named the Big Grass Fire in western Idaho and eastern Oregon.
WIDESpREAD FIRES
Spokane is not the only place struggling to contain fires.
Crews using bulldozers and helicopters continued for a 10th day to fight a fire that has burned about 525 square miles (about 1,360km2) of grassland in western Idaho and eastern Oregon. The area is home to cattle ranches, and authorities said the fire is threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures.
The weather in the area is expected to remain sunny — and dry — well into the week, with temperatures rising to more than 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32°C) by tomorrow. Officials say the fire was caused by lightning.
In central Utah, a massive blaze tripled in size over the weekend, jumping from 16 square miles (about 41km2) to about 56 square miles (145km2) by Sunday morning. More than 100 cattle have been killed, according to local law enforcement.
Officials called the fire “catastrophic” as high winds helped flames jump containment lines overnight. The fire is moving north toward Fillmore, a town of about 2,600 people and the seat of Millard County. Mandatory evacuations were ordered yesterday for the southern portion of Fillmore.
The US NWS issued warnings about the air quality across the northwest. It issued red flag fire warnings for parts of Utah and Montana and western Nebraska, and extreme heat warnings for the southern parts of Arizona, California and Nevada and northern Montana.

"Initially, we had approximately 290 missing person reports, and at this point we have cleared all except 14," Gregory said. "These may not all be specifically associated with the Spokane Complex Fires."

Entire Spokane neighborhoods lost homes. Chimneys that somehow withstood heat and flames were still standing like lone sentinels, symbols of what was there just a few days earlier.
Online efforts to help people swiftly popped up as friends of fire victims posted numerous appeals for money, clothes and basic necessities. Kory and MacKensie Aspaas were away with their children when the disaster hit.
"They are coming back from being out of town to a life that's been completely wiped out," friend Kali Butler said.

Spokane wildfires destroy hundreds of buildings as thousands evacuate
In what authorities have described as the largest natural disaster in the history of Spokane County, Washington, wildfires have destroyed hundreds of structures and forced the evacuation of thousands of people as firefighters continued their efforts to knock back and control several blazes in the area.
On Sunday, nearly 1,000 firefighters were combating at least three wildfires in Spokane, which is home to nearly 600,000 residents. More than 5,390 acres of land have been scorched, and officials said there was no containment of the fires Sunday afternoon.
ADVERTISING
Firefighters were racing to take advantage of weather conditions that had improved, but could worsen by Wednesday.
The National Weather Service said Sunday that wind gusts would increase after noon and ease after midnight and that conditions would remain very dry, which could propel wildfires into residential areas. Officials said that the danger from fires was still elevated, but that winds were weaker than those Saturday.
Officials have become increasingly concerned about the rapid spread of the wildfires and the significant risks they pose to populated communities in Spokane, one of the largest counties in Washington.
On Sunday, Gov. Bob Ferguson of Washington traveled to the area to speak with local officials, days after county officials urged residents in Level 3 evacuation zones — the highest level of evacuation order — to leave immediately. About 4,000 structures were at risk of burning.
Ferguson said that he spoke with President Donald Trump and Secretary Markwayne Mullin of the Department of Homeland Security, to express “how dire the situation is in Spokane and across our state.”
More than a dozen other fires were also burning across Washington, but most of those were in less populated areas, affecting about 250,000 acres. About 4,000 firefighters were working across the state.
“The President is aware of the situation, and expressed his concern for the people of Washington during this difficult time,” Ferguson said in a social media post on X, where he added that he hoped for a quick approval for the state’s request for a federal emergency declaration.
Videos on social media showed billowing smoke and orange-colored skies as cars in slow-moving traffic tried to get away from the fires. Others showed scorched communities, homes and vehicles.
Benjamin Cossel, the spokesperson for the California Interagency Incident Management Team 7, which began leading the firefighting effort Sunday morning after coming in from Oregon on Saturday, called the Spokane wildfires the “No. 1 priority fire in the nation,” because of its proximity to many homes.
The Old Trails and Autumn Lane fires jumped the Spokane River on Saturday and were encroaching on a nearby canyon Sunday, Cossel said, moving northwest away from the city of Spokane, but into the surrounding wilderness.
If the fire continues into the canyon, which local residents call Look Out Mountain, it could grow exponentially.
“The possibility for things to go sideways if it gets established in that canyon is pretty high,” he said, adding that “there is nothing really there to stop it.”
On Sunday, several aircraft dropped retardant and water on the flames.
Washington has been experiencing a record-breaking wildfire season, largely because of drought and heat. More than 1,000 fires have burned this year, covering about 425,000 acres, according to the Washington Department of Natural Resources.
On Saturday, forecasters with the National Weather Service had issued their most urgent alert — “a particularly dangerous situation” red-flag warning — for large parts of eastern Washington and northeastern Oregon. It marked the first time such a warning was issued in Washington, officials said.
Ferguson also declared a state of emergency across Washington, pointing to drought conditions, unusually high temperatures and strong winds.
Response resources from across the nation have been called on to combat this blaze, Cossel said, depleting already limited reserves.
“We have multiple large incidents across the nation,” Cossel said, “resources are absolutely tapped.”

UPDATE: August 3 at 8:21 a.m.
Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels emphasized on Monday that neighborhoods still under Level 3 evacuation orders are not safe and residents should stay away.
“Because of the weather conditions, because of the fire behavior, those homes could quickly be threatened and people could be in real danger," Nowels said. "If it’s a Level 3 evacuation area, please stay out. Let our firefighters do the work they need to do.”
Nowels also said people entering neighborhoods under Level 3 evacuation orders makes it harder to quickly identify looters or individuals doing “nefarious things.”
Additionally, more than 200 people called the Spokane County Sheriff's Office (SCSO) for evacuation after the fires broke out. Nowels said the sheriff's office has been able to account for all of them by phone except for 14.

More than 900 firefighters are working the Spokane Area Fires on Monday. That number is expected to grow to more than 2000 this week.

Nursing staff helped people change their clothes behind blankets. Some elders needed oxygen masks. People were talking in low voices, tired from not sleeping well in a crowded convention center.
Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said in a press conference that the state is working with the Federal Emergency Management Agency to get disaster assistance.

Fires near Spokane, WA have burned 600 structures and forced 60,000 evacuations
(AP) - Wildfires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area while destroying at least 600 homes, businesses and other structures, authorities said Sunday.
The fires in and around Spokane, the state’s second largest city, burned about 8.2 square miles (about 21 square kilometers) over the weekend and were among dozens of wildfires across the Western U.S. that stretched the ability of federal, state and local agencies to fight them.
A total of about 390 square miles (1,000 square kilometers) has burned across the state, and some of the fires, including those in the Spokane area, have not been contained.
No one hurt or unaccounted for — so far
Fire and law enforcement officials said there had been no reports of injuries or people unaccounted for — but they stressed it was early in the response effort.
Officials also said that the evacuees in Spokane included patients at its U.S. Veterans Affairs hospital.
Video from the Spokane area showed buildings on fire, black smoke billowing up near neighborhoods, and the smoking ruins of homes, with only chimneys still standing. Several officials expressed concern that the area does not appear likely to get a break in coming days from the weather, which is expected to remain dry.
“We are not out of danger,” U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell said during a news conference with federal, state and local officials in Spokane. “The next couple of days will be challenging.”
Investigators had yet to determine how the blazes started.
Grassland in flames in parts of Idaho and Oregon
Spokane was hardly the only place struggling to contain fires.
Crews using bulldozers and helicopters continued for a 10th day to fight a fire that has burned nearly 525 square miles (about 1,360 square kilometers) of grassland in western Idaho and eastern Oregon. The area is home to cattle ranches, and authorities said the fire is threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures.
The weather in the area was expected to remain sunny — and dry — well into the week, with temperatures rising to more than 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32 degrees Celsius) on Wednesday. Officials say the fire was caused by lightning.
In central Utah, a massive blaze more than doubled in size over the weekend, jumping from 16 square miles (about 41 square kilometers) to about 56 square miles (145 square kilometers) by Sunday morning. More than 100 cattle have been killed, according to local law enforcement.
Officials called the fire “catastrophic” as heavy winds helped flames jump containment lines overnight. The fire is moving north toward Fillmore, a town of about 2,600 people and the seat of Millard County. Mandatory evacuations were ordered Sunday evening for the southern portion of Fillmore.
The National Weather Service issued warnings about the air quality across the northwest. It issued red flag fire warnings for parts of Utah and Montana and western Nebraska, and extreme heat warnings for the southern parts of Arizona, California and Nevada and northern Montana.
High winds make it hard to fight fires in Spokane area
While temperatures Sunday in Spokane were forecast to remain below 80 F (27 C), wind gusts from 35 mph (56 kph) to 45 mph (72 kph) had been expected by the afternoon, said Benjamin Cossel, public information officer for the federal response team from California called in Saturday night to deal with the fires.
“We have weather working against us, and we have terrain working against us,” Cossel said.
There were three fires in the Spokane area: the Old Trails Fire, the Fairview Fire and the Meadowview Fire. Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency Saturday, and the National Weather Service issued a “particularly dangerous situation” red flag alert for eastern Washington.
Cossel said that as it gets warmer during the day, cool air that’s closer to the ground and keeping winds at bay will rise, allowing those winds to move through the area. The Spokane River cuts through the city of about 229,000 people, and there are steep canyons on both sides that channel the wind.
“They push the fire through the canyons, up, up the slopes, and then outside the slopes and around,” he said. “It’s very, very hilly, very, very steep slopes, a lot of canyons that create really turbulent, really challenging sort of wind scenarios.”
Spokane sets up shelter for impacted residents
Authorities in Spokane set up a shelter at the city’s main convention center. About 400 people were staying there, officials said Sunday.
Spokane County Commissioner Chris Jordan said relatives of his were in an area affected by the fires and that they don’t know if their home is still standing. He said he spoke with them as they were leaving the home.
“They’re in their car and all they can see is smoke everywhere, and it was incredibly scary for so many people,” he said during the news conference.
Heather Rosenstrater, president and CEO of Avista Corp., the area’s electric and natural gas utility, said about 10,000 people were without power Sunday, down from a peak of 30,000. Avista needs to repair two transmission lines, she said, so it’s possible that demand for electricity over the next few days could cause outages.
Meanwhile, several larger fires continued to burn in less populated areas northwest of Spokane, including one about 80 miles (129 kilometers) from the city that has burned about 210 square miles (544 square kilometers). Another fire in eastern Oregon, about 70 miles (113 kilometers) to the northwest in the Stinkingwater Mountains, has burned about 336 square miles (870 square kilometers).
“The whole northwest is heavily impacted right now,” said Keila Vizcarra, the spokesperson for the federal team from California handling what’s been named the Big Grass Fire in western Idaho and eastern Oregon.

Grassland in flames in parts of Idaho and Oregon

sources.news_title: More than a dozen wildfires burn in Washington state, forcing evacuations
sources.text:
Large parts of Spokane County, Washington, including residences and at least one hospital, were under mandatory evacuation orders Saturday as strong winds were propelling wildfires into residential areas.
At the same time, more than a dozen other fires were also burning across the state, mostly in less populated areas, affecting about 250,000 acres.
“This is an extraordinary fire season,” Dave Upthegrove, the state’s commissioner of public lands, said at a Saturday evening news briefing. “This is not normal.”
Nearly 3,000 acres in eastern Washington were burning late Saturday afternoon, pushed by wind gusts up to 45 mph, according to disaster tracking platform Watch Duty. The largest, the Old Trails fire, sparked around noon and had grown to about 2,500 acres by 5 p.m. local time.
Large parts of Spokane County were under the highest level of evacuation order, Level 3, and officials urged residents in the evacuation zone to leave immediately. Videos circulating on social media showed billowing smoke and orange-colored skies as cars in slow-moving traffic tried to get away from the fires. Officials said no injuries or deaths had been reported as of Saturday evening.
About 4,000 firefighters were working across the state to put out the fires, and the National Guard had also been deployed. Personnel or equipment from more than a dozen other states were also assisting, Upthegrove said.
Washington has been experiencing a record-breaking wildfire season, in part due to drought and heat. More than 1,000 fires have burned this year, covering about 425,000 acres, according to the Washington Department of Natural Resources.
On Saturday, forecasters with the National Weather Service had issued their most urgent alert — “a particularly dangerous situation” red-flag warning — for large parts of eastern Washington and northeastern Oregon. It marked the first time such a warning was issued in Washington, officials said.
Gov. Bob Ferguson also declared a statewide state of emergency, pointing to drought conditions, unusually high temperatures and strong winds.
In Spokane, about 4,000 structures were at risk of burning, according to George Geissler, the top forester in Washington state. A veterans hospital was evacuated, and all patients requiring ongoing medical care were sent to nearby hospitals, the hospital said on social media.
Mayor Lisa Brown of Spokane said that some city facilities, including a water treatment plant and a wastewater facility, had also been evacuated. An evacuation shelter was opened at the Spokane Convention Center.
Spokane County commissioners issued a disaster declaration during an emergency meeting Saturday evening.
About 28,000 Spokane-area customers of power company Avista were without power Saturday evening, Heather Rosentrater, the company’s CEO, said at the Spokane County commissioners’ meeting. She said that about 6,700 of those customers were without power because the company had proactively shut it off for safety reasons.
Officials said it was too early to determine the extent of the damage in Spokane.
“When the sun rises in the morning, I think we’re going to be in shock to see some of the scenes that emerge,” Maj. Gen. Gent Welsh, the Washington National Guard commander, said at the briefing. He called the situation “the roughest combination of series of events I’ve seen in my career.”
Spokane County’s sheriff, John Nowels, said that dangerous fire conditions were likely to persist for an additional 24 hours. He said it was unclear when evacuees would be able to return to their homes.

sources.news_title: Depending on your perspective, Spokane's worst fire happened Saturday
sources.text:
Depending on your perspective, Spokane’s worst fire happened Saturday
Only five weeks ago, a fire tore through Camp Sekani and into a neighborhood north of Spokane Valley, destroying 14 homes.
The Upriver fire killed one person and burned 213 acres.
That kind of wildfire, one that rips through an urban or suburban neighborhood burning a dozen or so houses, used to be rare during Spokane County’s fire seasons. There was the Valley View fire in 2008 that burned about 12 homes near Dishman Hills. The Hangman Hills fire in 1987 burned a couple dozen.
One used to stand out: A firestorm in October 1991 destroyed more than 100 homes in Spokane County. The Ponderosa Neighborhood in Spokane Valley was particularly hit hard.
But three years ago on Aug. 18, the Oregon Road fire in Elk destroyed 126 homes and the Gray fire on the West Plains and Medical Lake took 240.
That was only three years after 120 homes, most of the residences in the small town of Malden, were destroyed in northern Whitman County during the Babb Road fire, which started in Spokane County.
That kind of devastation intensified Saturday within Spokane city limits. The Old Trails fire started west of Spokane and blew into Northwest Spokane, burning 640 structures. Two other large fires in Spokane County burned homes, too, though officials hadn’t released the numbers of structures lost as of early Sunday afternoon.
As fires have intensified across the country and world in an era of climate change, firefighters have warned for many years that the kind of losses experienced on Saturday were possible, even likely, in Spokane.
Multiple officials on Sunday called the Old Trails fire the worst in the city of Spokane’s history. And by many measures, it is.
One fire might compete – at least in terms of total impact.
On Aug. 4, 1889, 32 blocks of downtown Spokane were destroyed in the Great Spokane Fire. It was an era when many cities were devastated and reborn in great fires, including Chicago, Seattle and Vancouver, British Columbia.
“All the banks, all the hotels, the post office, the land office, all the large business houses” were destroyed, the Spokane Falls Review reported soon after.

Around 60,000 residents faced mandatory evacuation orders as three fast-moving wildfires spread across Spokane, Washington, on August 2, 2026. The blazes scorched roughly 700 structures and burned over 5,000 acres, prompting emergency declarations and federal aid requests amid severe drought conditions.
A relentless combination of spiking temperatures, severe drought, and high winds drove three major wildfires into the northern edges of Spokane over the weekend, transforming quiet residential neighborhoods into fast-moving infernos. The Autumn Lane, Fairview, and Old Trails fires erupted and rapidly expanded, forcing about 60,000 people to evacuate their homes as flames jumped barriers and swept across the region.
Old Trails Fire Jumps the Spokane River and Threatens City Limits
The largest of the blazes, known as the Old Trails fire, started around noon on Saturday as a small vegetation fire in open brush and grass. Driven by strong winds, it raced north and east toward residential zones before jumping the Spokane River that afternoon, crossing directly into city limits and prompting the highest-level evacuation alerts across northern Spokane.
Public safety reporters on the ground witnessed the rapid escalation firsthand. I was sitting near an elementary school and saw a wall of flames east of the school and just a cascade of black smoke and a wall of flames coming toward me,
 Alexandra Duggan, a public safety reporter for The Spokesman-Review, described to NPR.
As traffic clogged escape routes and orange flames lit up the highway, residents scrambled to flee.
Mayor Lisa Brown Calls Blazes the Worst Regional Disaster in History
During a Sunday news conference alongside state and local emergency officials, Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown addressed the staggering toll of the disaster, labeling it the worst natural disaster our region has faced.
“Hundreds of homes and structures have been lost. We are still assessing the potential for lives to be lost.”
Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown, via Livemint
While damage assessments remained preliminary, state and local officials offered varying totals for the destruction. A spokesperson for the U.S. Forest Service put the number of destroyed structures at 600, while broader regional estimates from The Seattle Times cited approximately 700 structures consumed across roughly 8,000 acres, or 12 square miles.
Governor Bob Ferguson Declares State of Emergency and Requests Federal Assistance
In response to the crisis, Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a statewide emergency and implemented a burn ban, noting that the state was enduring its fourth straight year of drought. Across Washington, about more than 900 firefighters were battling a dozen major blazes that had scorched more than 250,000 acres.
The president was very gracious, I spoke to the president about what’s going on … and he expressed his support,
 Ferguson stated during the Sunday briefing.
Dave Upthegrove, the state’s public lands commissioner and head of the Department of Natural Resources, emphasized the unprecedented strain on firefighting resources. This is an extraordinary wildfire season in the Pacific Northwest,
 Upthegrove said, noting that crews from roughly a dozen states—ranging from Alaska to Florida—along with international support from Australia, had been deployed to assist.
Shelters Open as Avista Utilities Restores Power to Thousands
Spokane County Commissioner Chris Jordan noted that the Spokane County Fairgrounds had been specially prepared to accept residents with pets, livestock, and campers.
Avista Utilities CEO Heather Rosentrader reported that roughly 10,000 electricity customers lacked power on Sunday afternoon due to damaged utility lines and preventative public safety shutoffs initiated to mitigate elevated fire risks. Utility officials stated that power would be restored as soon as field conditions were verified as safe.
While weather conditions improved slightly on Sunday afternoon as winds began to ease, firefighting teams reported zero percent containment on the Spokane-area fires, leaving emergency personnel on high alert for changing weather patterns.
